interviewQuestions.question: Why can't mobile teams treat a release the same way a backend team treats a deploy?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core difference is that a backend deploy replaces the running code for everyone within minutes, while a mobile release only reaches users who choose to update — there's no mechanism to force it. The direct result is that at any given moment, your backend is serving a **mix of every client version shipped over the past several years**, not a clean before-and-after.

That single fact cascades into everything else about mobile release process. You go through a third party's app store review before any user sees the release, adding an external, variable-length delay you don't control. You stage rollouts by percentage rather than releasing to everyone at once, because a bug caught at 1% is cheap and a bug caught at 100% is not, and you can't roll back the way a backend does — you can only halt the rollout's growth and, if needed, flip a remote kill switch for the specific broken feature. And backend APIs serving mobile clients need years of backward compatibility, because you genuinely cannot fix an old client that's stuck out there; the only lever is not breaking it in the first place.

The mental shift I'd emphasize: on a backend, "we shipped the fix" and "the fix is live everywhere" are nearly the same statement. On mobile, they're never the same statement, and treating them as equivalent is the root cause of most mobile release incidents.

**Testing:** whether you understand the structural reason mobile release discipline differs, not just a list of practices without the underlying cause.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: A new feature ships and a week later crash reports spike for a subset of users. How would you respond, given you can't just redeploy like a backend service?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First move is to check whether the feature was released behind a remote flag. If it was, this is the best-case scenario: flip the flag off immediately, which takes effect within whatever your remote config's fetch interval is — typically minutes — with zero dependency on app store review. That stops the bleeding for every affected user, on whatever version they're on, without a new release.

If it wasn't flag-gated, the options narrow considerably. If the release is still mid-staged-rollout, I'd halt it immediately so exposure stops growing beyond whoever already has the bad version — that's damage control, not a fix, since users already on the new version keep the bug until a real fix ships. I'd then prioritize an emergency hotfix release, being explicit with the team that even an expedited store review isn't instant, so the honest timeline for full resolution might be a day or more, not minutes.

While that's in flight, I'd check whether the crash is isolable server-side at all — sometimes a backend-side mitigation (returning a different response shape that avoids triggering the client bug, or disabling a server-side capability the buggy code path depends on) can reduce impact even without touching the client.

The retrospective action item is always the same after an incident like this: any feature with meaningful blast radius should have shipped behind a flag in the first place — that's the actual lesson, not just "be more careful next time."

**Testing:** whether you understand the actual mitigation levers available on mobile and their real latency, rather than assuming a backend-style instant rollback exists.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Incident Response

interviewQuestions.question: Your backend team wants to change a core API's response format to unblock a new feature, but 8% of active traffic is still on app versions over a year old that expect the current format. How do you handle this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat this as a versioning problem, not a timing problem — waiting longer doesn't fix it, because that 8% isn't going away; it's largely users who are permanently stuck on old OS versions their devices can't upgrade past, or who simply don't update often. Any plan based on "they'll update eventually" is built on a false premise.

The approach: introduce the new response format as an additive change — a new field, or a versioned endpoint/response — rather than mutating the existing contract in place. Old clients keep reading the field shape they already understand and stay fully functional; new clients read the new shape and get the new feature. Both coexist on the same backend simultaneously, which is exactly the point.

I'd also push for the request to actually carry a client version, if it doesn't already, so this decision is based on real telemetry rather than a guess — knowing precisely that 8% is on versions from over a year ago, versus assuming it's negligible, changes how much engineering effort is worth spending on the compatibility path.

The old format only gets retired once telemetry shows that 8% (or whatever it's shrunk to) has dropped to a level the business is comfortable calling negligible, or — if it's not shrinking on its own — a deliberate decision to cut off unsupported versions via a minimum-version check, which is a product and support decision, not something to do silently through an API change.

**Testing:** whether you can design an additive migration path instead of reaching for a breaking change, and whether you think in terms of real telemetry rather than assumed adoption timelines.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: API Design

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer setting release standards for a mobile org, what would you require before any feature ships, and why?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd anchor the standards on the one fact that makes mobile releases different: you can't fix what's already out there, and you can't force anyone onto the new version. Everything I'd require flows from mitigating that.

First: any feature with meaningful blast radius or risk ships behind a remote flag, defaulted off, as a non-negotiable part of the release checklist — not a "nice to have for big features." The cost of adding a flag is small; the cost of a broken feature baked in with no kill switch is a multi-day incident bounded only by app store review speed.

Second: every rollout is staged with an explicit metrics threshold and an owner watching it at each stage, written down before the rollout starts, not decided reactively if something looks wrong. A staged rollout with no one watching provides none of its intended protection.

Third: any backend change touching an API that mobile clients call goes through a backward-compatibility review — does this break a client on a version from a year ago, and is there real telemetry on how much traffic that represents, not a guess. I'd want this enforced the same way a schema-migration review is enforced elsewhere: as a required check, not a courtesy.

Fourth: I'd track flag debt as a metric — flags left in the codebase past their rollout completion — because ungoverned flags are how a mobile codebase accumulates the kind of complexity that eventually makes every future change riskier to reason about.

The underlying principle I'd state explicitly to the org: on mobile, prevention is the only real lever, since there's no equivalent of a backend rollback — so process has to invest heavily upfront, not react after the fact.

**Testing:** whether you can turn the structural constraints of mobile releases into a concrete, enforceable set of org-level standards.
